title: Timeouts done right
summary: CancelAfter versus WaitAsync, HttpClient's own timeout, testable time with TimeProvider, and a time budget that degrades gracefully.

steps.title: Two kinds of timeout
body: **Cancel the work** (`CancelAfter` on a token you pass in): the operation itself stops, releasing the connection, the lock, the
database query. This is what you want almost always.
**Stop waiting for the work** (`task.WaitAsync(TimeSpan)`, .NET 6+): *you* get a `TimeoutException` after the time, but the
operation **keeps running** in the background, still holding whatever it holds. Use it only for operations that take no token.
```csharp fragment
using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2));
await client.GetAsync(url, cts.Token);            // the request is aborted at 2 s
await legacy.ComputeAsync().WaitAsync(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2));   // we stop waiting; ComputeAsync goes on
`HttpClient` has its own `Timeout` (default **100 seconds**, far too long for a service-to-service call): when it fires you get a
`TaskCanceledException` whose `InnerException` is a `TimeoutException`. In production, set timeouts per call with a resilience
pipeline (`Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience`, `AddStandardResilienceHandler()`): a total timeout, a per-attempt timeout and retries.

code: async Task SlowAsync() { await Task.Delay(1500); finished = true; }
steps.explain: `WaitAsync` abandoned the wait, not the work. `SlowAsync` kept running and finished later. In a server that is invisible load: work nobody is waiting for.

steps.prompt: A repository call takes a `CancellationToken`. You want it to give up after 300 ms. Which is right?
options: `using var cts = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(ct); cts.CancelAfter(300); await repo.LoadAsync(id, cts.Token);`
steps.explain: The linked source keeps the caller's cancellation *and* adds the deadline, and the query itself is cancelled. `WaitAsync` and `WhenAny` with a delay both leave the query running.

steps.title: Testable time: TimeProvider
body: Tests that really wait for timeouts are slow and flaky. .NET 8 added `TimeProvider`, an abstraction over the clock and timers that
the BCL accepts in the right places:
```csharp fragment
public sealed class Budget(TimeProvider time)
public CancellationTokenSource Start(TimeSpan limit) => new(limit, time);   // CTS that uses this clock
public Task Pause(TimeSpan d, CancellationToken ct) => Task.Delay(d, time, ct);
// production: new Budget(TimeProvider.System)
// tests:      var fake = new FakeTimeProvider();   (Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing)
//             fake.Advance(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3)); // the timeout fires now, no waiting
`PeriodicTimer`, `CancellationTokenSource`, `Task.Delay` and `Task.WaitAsync` all have `TimeProvider` overloads. Inject it like any
other dependency (`services.AddSingleton(TimeProvider.System)`).

steps.prompt: Match each API to what happens when its time is up.
pairs: the operation is cancelled and throws `OperationCanceledException`
the caller gets `TimeoutException`; the task keeps running
the token is cancelled when *that* clock says so (a fake one in tests)

steps.title: A time budget with a fallback
prompt: The product page asks the recommendations service for suggestions. It is nice to have, so it gets a **time budget**; if the budget
runs out, show `"(no recommendations)"`. But if the **client** disconnected, do not bother: let the cancellation propagate.
Write **`static async Task<string> WithBudgetAsync(Func<CancellationToken, Task<string>> call, TimeSpan budget, CancellationToken requestAborted)`**:
- run `call` with a token that is cancelled when **either** `requestAborted` is cancelled **or** `budget` elapses, and return its result;
- if it was cancelled because the **budget** ran out (and the request was not aborted), return `"(no recommendations)"`;
- if `requestAborted` was cancelled, let the `OperationCanceledException` out;
starter: static async Task<string> WithBudgetAsync(Func<CancellationToken, Task<string>> call, TimeSpan budget, CancellationToken requestAborted)
solution: static async Task<string> WithBudgetAsync(Func<CancellationToken, Task<string>> call, TimeSpan budget, CancellationToken requestAborted)
template: // A call that waits until its token is cancelled, and records that it saw the cancellation.
Dojo.Eq("A quick answer is returned", "books, pens", await WithBudgetAsync(_ => Task.FromResult("books, pens"), TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5), CancellationToken.None));
Dojo.Eq("When the budget runs out, the fallback is shown", "(no recommendations)", await WithBudgetAsync(DojoHang, TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(30), CancellationToken.None));
Dojo.Check("The call itself was cancelled, not just abandoned", dojoStopped, "Pass a token that the budget cancels into call(...); WaitAsync leaves the call running.");
await Dojo.ThrowsAsync<OperationCanceledException>("When the client disconnects, the cancellation propagates", () => dojoTask);
hints: `CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(requestAborted)` then `CancelAfter(budget)`, and pass its token to `call`.
explain: This shape (linked token, `CancelAfter`, exception filter on *which* token fired) is the core of every production timeout. Note the
